findings.title: Exhausted recovery-code credential from user storage is not actually removed
findings.body: The authenticator now resolves the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which returns the federated (user-storage) credential first when before it only looked at Keycloak's local store. When allCodesUsed() is true the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). That call only deletes from the local credential store; it does not remove or disable a credential owned by a user-storage provider. In addition, models built from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues (the shape the user-storage path produces) do not carry the original stored id, so getId() can be null and passing null into the credential store (JPA EntityManager.find) throws IllegalArgumentException. Consequence: for a user-storage user who exhausts all recovery codes the cleanup either throws or is silently ignored, the old federated credential stays in the user store, and it must be relied on that the subsequent required action overwrites it.

findings.title: Raw recovery codes are persisted to user storage while only hashed codes go local
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list and passes that JSON as the value of the UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...). If the user-storage provider persists the value it is handed (as the provided test provider does), the recovery codes are stored in cleartext in external storage. The local branch instead uses credentialModel, which contains only the hashed codes and per-code used flags (see RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.createFromValues). Recovery codes are single-use password-equivalent secrets, so storing them unhashed in an external user store is a meaningful exposure if that store leaks, and the asymmetry means the same credential has different representations depending on where it landed. The code should pass a hashed representation (or otherwise guarantee/require the provider hashes before persisting).

findings.title: User-storage recovery codes are replayable and single-use behavior is never exercised
findings.body: updateCredential stores the raw codes JSON, isValid compares input.getChallengeResponse() against that raw list without ever marking a code used, and getCredentials rebuilds the model with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(), which re-hashes the raw codes and sets every code's used flag back to false. As a result allCodesUsed() is always false, getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() always returns code #1, and a recovery code can be used repeatedly for a user in this provider. The new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin does only one login with the first code, so it does not cover the single-use guarantee or the 'all codes used -> re-configure' path. This both leaves the core security property of recovery codes untested and makes the test provider an unsafe model for real user-storage implementations.

findings.title: Recovery-codes credential cannot be disabled/removed in the user-storage test provider
findings.body: The provider now creates, validates and reports recovery-authn-codes as configured, but getDisableableCredentialTypesStream() still only adds CredentialModel.OTP and disableCredentialType() only handles OTP (it logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type: ...' for anything else). Consequently once a recovery-codes credential is written into this user storage it cannot be disabled through the admin or account credential APIs, and that removal path is never tested, so a broken/compromised/exhausted credential cannot be cleaned up.
